name: Resume design
routing_text: How should a software engineer or data scientist write their resume? Bullet points, professional summary, page length, formatting and layout, ATS keyword matching, quantified impact and metrics, tailoring a CV to one job description, and what a recruiter looks for in the seconds they spend skimming it.
blurb: What a technical resume has to do on the page before anyone reads it closely.

units.title: Tailor resumes for ATS with quantified impact
units.summary: The creators agree that strong tech resumes must be tailored to each job description, using keywords extracted from the posting while keeping formatting simple enough for ATS scanners. They recommend tools like ChatGPT prompts to generate keyword lists, VMock or open-source parsers for feedback, plain layouts without columns/graphics/tables, and quantified achievements plus GitHub or project links. They differ on emphasis: some say keyword matching is essential, while one recruiter argues hiring teams hunt for full qualifications in sentences, not isolated keywords. Another creator questions whether every quantified bullet is genuinely truthful, though concedes it can still impress recruiters.

units.title: resume, LinkedIn profile, recruiters, linkedin, keywords, ATS
units.summary: Recruiters are looking for agentic systems experience, not generic terms like semantic queries. A resume with typos will not have its projects checked by recruiters. Referrals are the social proof that tells recruiters you have worked with former colleagues. Hiring managers care about the impact you made, not just your responsibilities.

units.title: Tailor resumes to pass recruiters and ATS
units.summary: These creators argue that resumes are marketing documents aimed at a hiring manager's current problems, not full life stories. They advise highlighting the last five to seven years, limiting older roles to a few relevant bullet points, and mirroring job-description keywords to get past ATS scanners. Clean, consistent formatting—like balanced spacing, clear section breaks, and a professional title—is treated as essential for making a quick impression. They disagree on length: some insist on one page, while others show two-page layouts with continuation headers, and a few warn against relying on AI-generated content.

units.title: AI engineer, AI engineering, rag, LLM, prompt engineering, data scientist
units.summary: The job market is tough for software engineers, so resumes must be on point. An AI engineer requires AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred), C, and Java. For an AI engineer resume, projects should highlight LLMs, APIs, embeddings and the latest tools like LangChain. You must take ownership of ambiguous problems and drive them from ideation to solution without waiting for instructions.

units.title: LinkedIn SEO and keywords attract recruiter interviews
units.summary: The creators agree that treating LinkedIn as a search engine for recruiters is the key to getting job interviews, not just having a resume. They recommend packing the headline, about, experience, and skills sections with the exact job titles, tools, technologies, and industry terms recruiters search for, and customizing the LinkedIn URL for visibility. Tactics recur across the excerpts: turning off profile update notifications, setting Open to Work to recruiters only, adding up to 100 relevant skills from job postings, and sharing visible projects or portfolio links. One creator notes that resumes with a LinkedIn link see a 71% better response, while another cautions that broadcasting an unemployed status can weaken bargaining power, so those signals should be limited to recruiters.

units.title: fastapi, Python, Java, ai automation stack, FrontEnd, object-oriented programming
units.summary: In the skill section of a resume, write how you apply knowledge using Python with numpy, pandas, and scikit-learn, deployment with Flask and FastAPI, and cloud with AWS EC2 and AWS S3. The resume tool added C++ to the skill section. An AI engineer requires AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred), C, and Java. The degree on the resume is good.

rubrics.criterion: Write every experience bullet as a full qualification: what you did, how you did it, the result, and the context it happened in.
rubrics.check: For each bullet, identify all four parts: action, method/tool, outcome/result, and context (where or who it helped). If any bullet misses one of these parts, fail the resume.
rubrics.why: Recruiters hunt for qualifications, not bare tasks; without the result and context they don't know what you did or why it mattered and you don't get considered.
rubrics.unit_title: Tailor resumes for ATS with quantified impact

rubrics.check: Go down the skills section; for each skill, point to a linked repo/report or a project bullet that explains how you used it. Any skill with no supporting proof fails the resume.
rubrics.why: A bare claim looks careless and unfinished; proof is what makes a resume read like an engineer's work rather than a student's homework.

rubrics.criterion: Put the strongest, most relevant signal in the first page's five-to-seven-second scan zone and don't bury it under old roles or page two.
rubrics.check: Set a seven-second timer and skim the first page; if you cannot state the candidate's target role and one concrete result, fail. Also fail if the strongest result appears only on a later page or under an irrelevant older role.
rubrics.why: If the reader isn't hooked in five to seven seconds they move on; recruiters are scanning for signals, not reading a life story.
rubrics.unit_title: Tailor resumes for ATS with quantified impact

rubrics.criterion: Substantiate at least 75% of the job's required skills in experience or project bullets, not only in a skills section.
rubrics.check: Compare the required skills from the job posting against the resume; fail if 25% or more of those required skills appear only in the skills section or not at all in the experience/project bullets.
rubrics.why: Recruiters hunt for qualifications, not keyword lists, so skills that only sit in a section read as keywords and do not prove the applicant can do the job.

rubrics.criterion: Write every experience bullet as a demonstrated result instead of a vague list of duties.
rubrics.check: Look at each bullet under experience and check whether it names a concrete outcome or impact such as a percentage, a cost, a timeline, or a delivered system; fail if the bullet only describes responsibilities in general terms.
rubrics.why: Vague, task-only bullets make the resume feel risky and get it rejected, while result bullets show the reader you have already done the job and can do it again.

rubrics.criterion: Link every serious project to a public, professional artifact such as GitHub, a blog post, or a personal website, and keep that artifact clean and secure.
rubrics.check: Click each link in the resume. For each GitHub repo, verify it has a README, a requirements.txt file, clean code folders, and no public .env file or API keys; fail the resume if any link is broken, the repo is empty, or a secret is exposed.
rubrics.why: Industry professionals use GitHub only, and exposed secrets or messy repos make a recruiter distrust the candidate with production data.
